A.biggest_strength: Structured 5-scene pedagogical narrative that explicitly isolates the core halving insight with a 'dropped' bracket visual, complemented by thorough engineering notes on real-world edge cases (integer overflow, duplicates, half-open ranges).
A.biggest_weakness: Array cells cannot be clicked directly to choose a search target, and at 390 px mobile width Scene 5 suffers a text collision between the scale chart header and the multiplication callout note.
A.interaction_feedback: Stepping through the algorithm using the range scrubber, step buttons, presets, and keyboard shortcuts (arrows, comma/period) felt seamless and responsive. The live calculation accurately reflected custom targets like 26 and missing elements like 40. However, clicking array cells directly does nothing (a reader naturally expects to click a cell to find it), and entering Scene 3 directly triggers an automated sweep unless manually paused.

Navigated through scenes 1 to 4 using scene navigation buttons
Stepped through all search steps 0 to 7 for target 37 using Next Step (›) button
Stepped backward to step 6 using Previous Step (‹) button
Tested preset '79 most compares' and scrubbed to step 9 (found at index 15 in 5 compares)
Tested preset '40 missing' and scrubbed to step 8 (verified low > high termination)
Entered custom target 26 via input field and verified found state at index 5 in 3 compares
Tested Play tour button (watched animated playback and paused)
Tested keyboard navigation: ArrowRight/ArrowLeft for scenes, ArrowUp/ArrowDown and comma/period for stepping
Scrolled and inspected notes section, implementation code, comparison table, and terms glossary
Evaluated mobile layout at 390 px width across all scenes and notes
Evaluated reduced motion mode (--reduced) verifying instantaneous transition to resting state
Tested dark mode appearance (--theme dark)

B.biggest_strength: Direct tactile interactivity with clickable array cells, live synchronized code-line highlighting, and an interactive logarithmic slider (1 to 1 billion) featuring a dynamic, to-scale halving ladder.
B.biggest_weakness: Wrapping the 32-element array into an 8x4 grid at mobile widths breaks the 1D spatial intuition of binary search, causes pointer tags (like 'hi') to visually collide with cells in the row above, and disconnects from the 1D funnel bar below.
B.interaction_feedback: Clicking cells directly in the array to launch a search is delightful and intuitive. Stepping forward and backward with buttons or Arrow keys while watching the Python code highlight line-by-line provides immediate clarity. The logarithmic slider in Figure 2 gives a dramatic visual sense of O(log n) efficiency. However, on phone widths (390 px), the 4-row grid wrap makes pointer labels ambiguous and obscures the left/right partition concept.

structured_output.reasons: Page A is the overall winner because its pedagogical architecture builds a stronger, more disciplined mental model for a programming blog post. Its 5-scene progression breaks the algorithm into digestible conceptual milestones, most notably Scene 3 ('Drop a half'), which uses an explicit visual bracket to show why sorted order permits discarding half the candidates in a single comparison. Furthermore, Page A preserves the 1D spatial integrity of the array on mobile devices and includes critical software engineering context (integer overflow in mid calculation, duplicate values, lower bounds, and half-open ranges). While Page B offers fantastic tactile features—such as clickable array cells and an interactive logarithmic scale slider up to 1 billion elements—its decision to wrap the array into a 4-row grid on mobile severely degrades the visual metaphor of binary search and causes pointer tag misplacement.
